abstract: The cuticular lipids of insects serve both as a barrier against desiccation and as chemical signals. In social insects, these lipids regulate reproduction and nestmate recognition, potentially creating a trade-off between waterproofing and communication. We tested this hypothesis in bumblebee workers by examining the roles of cuticular compounds in desiccation resistance and behavioral attraction. Desiccation survival varied with age, social state, and ovary activation, with fertile queenless workers showing the greatest resistance. Cuticular profiles changed markedly with age and social environment. Although the total amount of secretion remained similar among groups, queenright workers showed age-dependent decline in alkenes and a corresponding increase in two acetate esters (tetracosyl and hexacosyl acetate). To determine the functions of these compounds, we tested their effects on desiccation survival and attraction. Topical application of several hydrocarbons, but not tetracosyl acetate, increased desiccation resistance. In contrast, tetracosyl acetate, but not hydrocarbons, elicited attraction, and only in queenright workers. These results demonstrate an age-dependent shift in cuticular lipid composition in the presence of the queen from producing waterproofing hydrocarbons toward signaling compounds in the presence of the queen, reducing desiccation resistance while enhancing communication. Our findings suggest that the evolution of insect cuticular lipids has been shaped by both physiological demands and selection for complex social communication.
